title: Why 23 people are enough for a shared birthday

beats.title: Why 23 people are enough
beats.subtitle: A fifty percent coincidence, once you count pairs
beats.narration: Twenty-three people in one room. The chance that two of them share a birthday is about fifty percent. That sounds impossible, so let's count it properly.
beats.notes: Open on the number, not the formula: 23 people, 50% is the whole puzzle.

beats.heading: The claim
beats.subheading: 365 equally likely days, 23 people, one shared birthday
beats.narration: Assume three hundred sixty-five equally likely days, and ignore leap years. The question is whether any two people in the group match, not whether someone matches a particular person.
beats.notes: Pinning the assumptions here keeps the later arithmetic honest. The word any is the hinge.

beats.heading: Why it feels impossible
beats.narration: The usual mistake is to compare one person with the other twenty-two. That gives twenty-three small chances, about six percent in total. It also quietly assumes the question names somebody.
beats.notes: Name the wrong model before replacing it; the viewer will recognise their own reasoning.

beats.heading: Count pairs, not people
items: Every two people form one pair
Each pair is its own coincidence
beats.narration: So count pairs instead of people. Every two people form one pair, and twenty-three people form twenty-three times twenty-two divided by two: two hundred fifty-three pairs. Each pair is a separate chance of a coincidence.
beats.notes: The pivot of the episode: 253 comparisons is the quantity that grows, not 23 people.

beats.heading: The exact chance
beats.narration: Here is the exact probability against group size. It starts flat, then bends upward, because each newcomer pairs with everyone already in the room. At twenty-three people the curve crosses one half.
beats.notes: The graph earns its place by showing a rate change: the curve is flat at first, then accelerates. The crossing at 23 is a limit the viewer can see, not a number to trust.

beats.heading: Why the curve bends
beats.narration: The exact count is easier by complement. The chance that nobody matches is a product of shrinking fractions: three sixty-five over three sixty-five, then three sixty-four over three sixty-five, and so on. Subtract that product from one, and at twenty-three people you get fifty point seven percent.
beats.notes: Derive, do not announce: the product is the no-match path, and subtracting it from one is the complement rule.

beats.heading: Where the intuition failed
beats.narration: So the intuition was not wrong about days. It was wrong about pairs. Twenty-three people look small next to three hundred sixty-five days, yet they create two hundred fifty-three comparisons.
beats.notes: The comparison is between two models of the same situation, not two facts.

beats.heading: What we established
items: Pairs grow with the square of the group
beats.narration: Three things to keep. First, pairs grow with the square of the group, so intuition fails early: those twenty-three people already form two hundred fifty-three pairs. Second, counting the complement is easier than counting matches, because nobody matching is a single product, not a pile of cases. Third, the two landmarks worth remembering are twenty-three people for half, and fifty-seven for ninety-nine percent.
beats.notes: Restate the mechanism, then the two landmark numbers, with enough air to read the list.

beats.heading: Next question
beats.next: Where else does counting pairs beat counting people?
